criteria.descriptor: Full marks for statistically and methodologically correct claims: signal-vs-noise on 300 judge scores handled with a paired test/CI and power/MDE; correct account of aggregate masking (Simpson-style) and worst-slice gating; accurate treatment of LLM-judge bias, calibration and versioning; correct offline-vs-online distinction; and sound canary/guardrail/rollback mechanics. Deduct for fabricated statistics, treating the judge as ground truth, or mischaracterising how canarying works.

Full marks cover both halves: a diagnosis spanning statistical invalidity, segment masking, stale/unrepresentative golden set, and judge validity; AND a design spanning stratified/powered pre-release gating plus continuous evaluation (canary, sliced guardrail metrics, online sampling, drift detection, automatic rollback, loop closure). Partial credit if either the diagnosis or the online-evaluation design is thin or missing.

Full marks explain WHY each flaw let this specific product-line regression slip through and why each proposed control would have caught it (e.g. worst-slice gating vs averaged mean, canary against escalation vs an offline proxy), and weigh real trade-offs (velocity/cost vs rigor, judge vs human, canary sample size vs detection time). Lower marks for asserted fixes without causal linkage to the observed failure.

Full marks for a well-organised diagnosis-then-design answer at a senior design-review register, using the vocabulary precisely (paired test, power/MDE, stratification, faithfulness/groundedness, judge calibration, canary, guardrail, drift, rollback). Lower marks for vague, disorganised, or jargon-dropping prose that does not make the mechanisms legible.

expected_answer_points: The gate reads a point estimate with no uncertainty; a 0.05 move on 300 stochastic judge scores is likely within noise, so it needs a paired significance test / bootstrap confidence interval and a defined minimum detectable effect (power analysis).

A single aggregate mean masks per-segment regressions (Simpson-style effect); the fix is stratified evaluation by segment (esp. product line) with gating on the worst-slice delta, an eval set representative of production traffic, and multiple-comparison awareness.

The frozen golden set is stale and under-covers the failing product line; it must be continuously refreshed from production, mined for hard/failure cases, and grow a permanent regression case from every incident.

Critiques the LLM-as-judge: a coarse single pointwise score, judge biases (verbosity/position/self-preference) and judge drift; requires calibration against human labels, a pinned/versioned judge, and decomposition into faithfulness/groundedness/relevance/safety.

Argues offline pre-release evaluation is structurally insufficient -- a proxy on a fixed sample that cannot see live distribution shift or the true business outcome (escalation rate); the gate is a filter, not a guarantee.

Designs continuous/online evaluation: canary/shadow/A-B rollout instead of 100%, guardrail metrics (escalation, thumbs-down, handoff) sliced by segment, online judge/human sampling of live traffic, drift detection, alerting and automatic rollback.

Closes the loop and weighs trade-offs: incident -> root cause -> add to regression suite; notes feedback-loop contamination risk for retraining and balances rigor against release velocity and human-eval cost.
common_pitfalls: Treats 4.20 -> 4.25 as a genuine improvement and never asks whether the delta exceeds judge noise -- no confidence interval, significance test, or power analysis.
Proposes only a bigger golden set or a better judge prompt, without stratification, representativeness, or worst-slice gating, so the same segment-masking recurs.
Trusts the LLM-as-judge as ground truth: no human calibration, no acknowledgement of judge bias or drift, and no pinning/versioning of the judge model and prompt.
Keeps gating on an aggregate metric and merely tightens the 0.1 threshold, so a single-segment regression is still averaged away.

Stops at pre-release evaluation with no online/canary guardrail on the real business metric (escalation rate) and no automatic rollback, so nothing catches a distribution the offline set does not contain.
Recommends blocking every release behind full human evaluation, ignoring cost and velocity trade-offs and the fact that human review does not scale to continuous monitoring.
reference_answer:
The gate failed because it compresses everything into one noisy aggregate and never leaves the offline world.

Diagnosis. (1) No uncertainty: a 4.20->4.25 move on 300 items scored by a stochastic judge is almost certainly within noise, yet the gate reads a bare point estimate. Because the same items are scored before and after, use a paired comparison (paired bootstrap or Wilcoxon on per-item score deltas) and gate on the confidence interval, plus a power analysis defining a minimum detectable effect (e.g. -0.15); 300 items may lack the power to see a regression you care about. (2) Aggregation masks segments: a mean can rise while one subpopulation collapses (a Simpson-style effect). The failing product line is a slice whose few examples were swamped. (3) The frozen golden set is stale and unrepresentative -- it under-covers, or omits, that product line, so no amount of aggregate scrutiny could surface it. (4) LLM-as-judge validity: a single pointwise 1-5 holistic score is coarse, and the judge is itself a model with verbosity/position/self-preference bias and its own drift; it was never calibrated against human labels, and if the judge prompt/model isn't pinned, a 'improvement' could be judge drift. (5) Structural limit: offline eval measures a proxy on a fixed sample and cannot see live distribution shift or the true business outcome -- escalation rate -- which is an online signal.

Design. Pre-release: stratify the eval set by product line, query type, difficulty, language, and retrieval hit/miss; make it representative of (or reweighted to) live traffic; report per-slice deltas and gate on the worst regressing slice with multiple-comparison correction and enough items per slice for power. Replace the single score with decomposed, largely reference-based metrics -- faithfulness/groundedness to retrieved context, answer relevance, correctness, safety -- and pin+version the judge, whose agreement with human labels (correlation / Cohen's kappa) is tracked. Continuously refresh the set from production, mine hard/failure cases, and add every incident as a permanent regression case (this failure becomes a fixed test).

Continuous evaluation: never ship straight to 100%. Roll out via shadow or canary / A-B with automatic guardrail metrics -- escalation/handoff rate, thumbs-down, deflection -- and an online judge/human score on a sampled stream of real traffic, all sliced by the same segments, with alerting and automatic rollback on a guardrail breach. Add input/output drift detection and spend a human-review budget on sampled live traffic to keep the judge honest. On breach: roll back, root-cause, feed the case into the golden set, and guard against feedback-loop contamination if that data also trains the model.

Net trade-off: keep the pre-release gate but make it stratified, paired, powered, and judge-calibrated -- and accept it is a filter, not a guarantee. The escalation regression is ultimately caught in production by canarying against the real business metric with fast automatic rollback, which is cheaper and safer than trying to make an offline set omniscient.
